newsitem.title: USA: Ford confirms new Lincoln sedan coming in 1999.
newsitem.headline: Ford confirms new Lincoln sedan coming in 1999.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. has finally put a due date on the new baby Lincoln car that industry analysts have been talking about for years: early 1999.

The new rear-wheel drive Lincoln announced Sunday will come in two versions, the LS6 and LS8. The names stand for luxury sedan and correspond to the six-cylinder and eight-cylinder engines it will offer.

The five-passenger LS is being built off an all-new platform that is also being used for the new Jaguar X200, which is also owned by Ford. The LS will be similar in size to a BMW 5-Series, and will be sold in Europe about the same time as it goes on sale in the U.S.
Officials from Ford's luxury vehicle division say the new arrival will take years off the average age of the traditional Lincoln buyer, which now hovers at 67 years old.

The LS is designed to appeal to people in their mid-30s to late-40s. An estimated 35 percent to 40 percent are expected to be women, up from the 18 percent to 20 percent of cars that now typically go to women. First-time luxury car buyers, many of whom would normally buy imports, are seen accounting for 60 percent of the sales.

Lincoln-Mercury General Manager James O'Connor would not discuss pricing for the new car Monday. Christopher Cedergren, managing director of automotive consultant Nextrend, predicts the LS6 will start around $30,000, with the V-8 version going for about $42,000. The lower end would make it the least expensive vehicle in the Lincoln lineup.

Although the 77-year-old brand has a reputation for comfort and quality, it has suffered from sluggish sales for years, and remains largely distinguished by the Town Car, a smooth-riding mammoth that is a favorite among older men.
O'Connor said the LS cars are the latest indications of a revived Lincoln brand that is emerging from the U.S. No. 2 automaker.

"What we're finding is while our traditional buyer is in their 60s, people who are younger know what Lincoln is, but they didn't particularly care for the product. It just didn't appeal to them," he said.

But the fast success of the new Navigator shows people are starting to see Lincoln in a new light, according to O'Connor. Lincoln currently has seven months' worth of orders for the full-size sport utility vehicle. Many Navigator buyers are in their 40s and 50s. Celebrity buyers include hockey star Wayne Gretzky.
"We believe we're broadening the relevancy of the product line, so we continue to retain our older customers and go after younger ones," he said.
Lincoln car sales through July are down 4 percent, but Navigator sales have pushed total Lincoln sales up 4 percent over last year to 80,631.

Cedergren said it remains to be seen how quickly younger buyers embrace a new car from a traditional American luxury brand. An attempt by General Motors Corp's Cadillac to woo a younger crowd with the Catera has not met expectations, he said. More than 50 percent of Catera buyers are over 60 years old.
Another challenge is Lincoln's tradition-minded dealer body, he said.
"I think the product probably is going to be damn good. The only negative is the Lincoln brand name, which has a stigma of being old," he said.

Ford will build the LS cars at its Wixom, Mich., large car assembly plant west of Detroit. The platform, known by the code named DEW, will also be used for several new products. They include the next-generation Thunderbird, Mustang, and possibly a future Mark VIII, said Cedergren.
